newsitem.title: USA: Philip Morris, AT&T top campaign donors list - report.
newsitem.headline: Philip Morris, AT&T top campaign donors list - report.

text.p: Tobacco company Philip Morris, communications firm AT&T, a trial lawyers' group and the Teamsters Union are the top contributors to U.S. political campaigns, researchers reported on Thursday.

Rounding out the top 10 donors were four more unions, the American Medical Association and RJR Nabisco, another tobacco company, according to the Center for Responsive Politics, which relied on the Federral Election Commission's figures.
"We have a political system paid for by Wall Street, not Main Street, and some might say by Tobacco Road," Ellen Miller, executive director of the center, said at a news conference.
All of the top four contributors gave more than $2 million each to various races and parties, primarily over a period from January 1995 through June 1996, the center said.
Philip Morris topped the list with a total of $2.74 million and AT&T gave $2.13 million, with most of their donations going to Republicans.
The Association of Trial Lawyers of America gave $2.10 million and the Teamsters gave $2.09 million, with the bulk of the money going to Democrats.

Also in the Top 10, in descending order, were the Laborers Union, the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, RJR Nabisco, the National Education Association, the American Medical Association and the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees.

Researchers counted money donated to political action committees, which went mostly to congressional campaigns, as well as so-called "soft money" donations to national political parties, and large donations by PACs and individuals to the presidential campaigns of Republican Bob Dole and President Bill Clinton.

Political giving tended to divide along party lines, with labor unions and lawyers consistently backing Democrats and business groups giving heavily to Republicans. But most donors spent money on both parties, however lopsidedly.

The presidential race between President Clinton, a Democrat, and Republican challenger Bob Dole will cost about $800 million, Miller said, with the total price tag for all U.S. federal elections exceeding $1.6 billion.

Business groups donated most, with a total of $242 million in donations, nearly seven times the $35 million given by labor groups and more than $10.6 million given by ideological groups -- such as the National Rifle Association, which opposes gun control, and the Human Rights Campaign, which supports homosexual rights.

There was a clear shift in giving after Republicans won a majority of seats in Congress in November 1994, the center said. As Republicans took pivotal seats on Capitol Hill, more money flowed toward them and less toward congressional Democrats.
The center is a non-profit, non-partisan research organization that focuses on Congress and the role money plays in congressional elections.
